subject: combined-science

items.q: A long straight vertical wire carries a steady current. What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around the wire?
items.correct: Circles centred on the wire and lying in a plane at right angles to it
items.misconception: Straight lines that spread out from the wire, like spokes on a wheel
items.why: Radial patterns are met first, in diagrams of light spreading from a lamp and of the field around a point charge, and that picture is reused for the wire. Plotting compasses placed around the wire do not point away from it; they line up end to end and trace closed circles around it. Magnetic field lines are closed loops and never start or end on the wire.
items.random_wrong: Straight lines running parallel to the wire along its whole length

items.q: A plotting compass is moved from 2 cm to 6 cm away from a wire carrying a steady current. The current is not changed. What happens to the deflection of the compass?
items.correct: It gets smaller, because the field is weaker further from the wire
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the current through the wire is unchanged
items.why: Current is the quantity asked about most often, so distance is treated as scenery rather than as a variable. The specification states that the strength of the field depends on the current through the wire AND the distance from the wire. On a field diagram the circles are drawn further apart further out, which is how a weaker field is shown.
items.random_wrong: It falls to zero, because the field stops at the outer circle

items.q: A student winds a straight wire into a solenoid and passes the same current through it as before. What happens to the magnetic field produced?
items.correct: It is stronger, because the fields of the turns add together
items.misconception: It is weaker, because the current now has a longer path to run
items.why: Longer wire is associated with higher resistance and with things running down, so longer is read as weaker. Shaping the wire does not use the current up, and the current is set by the circuit. Each turn contributes its own field in the same direction inside the coil, so the fields add and the effect is much stronger.
items.random_wrong: It is unchanged, because the current in the wire is unchanged

items.q: What best describes the magnetic field inside a long solenoid that is carrying a current?
items.correct: Strong and uniform, drawn as evenly spaced parallel lines
items.misconception: Strong at the very centre of the coil and almost zero elsewhere
items.why: Fields met earlier, around a wire or around a pole, weaken with distance from one place, so a single strongest point is expected. Field lines drawn inside a solenoid are straight, parallel and evenly spaced along its length, which is exactly how a uniform field is shown. Iron filings inside a long coil line up the same way all along it.
items.random_wrong: A set of circles running round the axis, as around a straight wire

items.q: How does the magnetic field around the outside of a current-carrying solenoid compare with that of a bar magnet?
items.correct: It has a similar shape, with one end acting as a north pole and one as a south
items.misconception: It is a set of circles around the middle of the coil, not like a bar magnet
items.why: The circular pattern around a straight wire is learned first and is carried over to the coiled wire unchanged. Each turn does produce circles around its own wire, but inside the coil those circles all point the same way along the axis and add together, while outside them they largely cancel. The result inside is a straight, uniform field.
items.random_wrong: It has exactly the same shape, but the ends of a solenoid are not poles

items.q: An iron core is placed inside a solenoid that is carrying a current. What is the effect?
items.correct: The magnetic field of the solenoid becomes considerably stronger
items.misconception: The solenoid begins to produce a magnetic field for the first time
items.why: Classroom electromagnets almost always have a core, so the core looks like the part that does the work. An air-cored solenoid deflects a compass held at its end, showing that a field is already present. The core is magnetised by that field and adds its own, which is why the total field becomes much stronger.
items.random_wrong: The field grows stronger and stays on after the current is off

items.q: Which observation best demonstrates that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field?
items.correct: A compass beside the wire swings round when the current is switched on
items.misconception: A plotting compass beside the wire keeps pointing north when the current is off
items.why: Deflection of a compass is associated with magnets, so a magnet is assumed to be needed before anything can happen. The whole point of the demonstration is that no magnet is present. The compass swings when the current is switched on and returns to north when it is switched off, so the current alone is producing the field.
items.random_wrong: The wire becomes noticeably warmer when the current is switched on

items.q: The direction of the current in a straight wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field pattern?
items.correct: The circles stay, but the arrows point the other way round
items.misconception: The pattern and the arrows on it are both completely unchanged
items.why: Field strength is the quantity attended to, and strength does not depend on which way the current flows. Direction is set by the direction of the current, through the right-hand grip rule. A plotting compass placed by the wire visibly swings through 180° when the connections are swapped over.
items.random_wrong: The circles turn into straight lines pointing back along the wire

items.q: A student is asked to draw the magnetic field of a current-carrying solenoid, showing its direction. Which drawing is correct?
items.correct: Closely spaced parallel arrows inside the coil, looping outside from north to south
items.misconception: Parallel lines inside the coil and loops outside it, with no arrows on any line
items.why: Marks are associated with the shape of the drawing, and direction feels like a detail rather than part of the answer. A field has a direction at every point, defined as the direction in which a compass north pole points. Without arrows the diagram does not say whether the field runs clockwise or anticlockwise, so it is incomplete.
items.random_wrong: Parallel arrows inside the coil that start at one end and stop at the other

items.q: Why does winding a wire into a solenoid increase the magnetic effect of the current?
items.correct: The field of each turn points the same way inside the coil, so they add up
items.misconception: Winding the wire into a coil increases the current flowing in it
items.why: A stronger effect is equated with more current, since current is the quantity known to control the field. An ammeter in the circuit shows the current is unchanged, or very slightly smaller because of the extra resistance. What changes is that many turns now contribute their fields at the same place.
items.random_wrong: The coiled wire has a much larger resistance, and that strengthens the field

items.q: A relay diagram shows a coil wound on an iron core in one circuit, and a pivoted iron armature that closes contacts in a second circuit. How does the relay work?
items.correct: A small current magnetises the core, so the armature closes the contacts
items.misconception: The current in the coil flows on through the contacts and into the second circuit
items.why: The two circuits are drawn close together on the diagram, and one connected path is the usual picture of a circuit. Tracing the wires shows that the coil circuit is a complete loop on its own. The only link between the circuits is magnetic, which is why a relay lets a small safe current switch a large one.
items.random_wrong: The magnetised iron core repels the armature and pushes it onto the contacts

items.q: A wire carrying a current is held at right angles to the field between the poles of a magnet. Which statement about the forces is correct?
items.correct: The magnet and the wire each exert a force on the other
items.misconception: Only the wire feels a force, as the magnet carries no current
items.why: Only the wire is seen to move in demonstrations, because the magnet is heavy and is usually clamped down. Forces always come in pairs. The specification says the magnet and the conductor exert a force on each other; stand the magnet on a balance and its reading changes when the current is switched on.
items.random_wrong: Only the magnet feels a force, because it produces the field

items.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what do the first finger, the second finger and the thumb represent?
items.correct: The first finger the field, the second finger the current, and the thumb the force
items.misconception: The first finger is the current, the second the field, the thumb the motion
items.why: The two fingers look alike and the initial letters are not attached to them, so the pairing is guessed. The letters are the memory aid: First-Field, seCond-Current, thuMb-Motion. Swapping the two fingers reverses the predicted force, turning a right answer into a wrong one.
items.random_wrong: The first finger is the force, the second the field, and the thumb current

items.q: A horizontal wire carries a current from left to right. The magnetic field between the poles is directed into the page. In which direction is the force on the wire?
items.correct: Upwards, at right angles to both the current and the field
items.misconception: Downwards, at right angles to both the field and the current
items.why: The two fingers look alike and the initial letters are not attached to them, so the pairing is guessed. The letters are the memory aid: First-Field, seCond-Current, thuMb-Motion. Swapping the two fingers reverses the predicted force, turning a right answer into a wrong one.
items.random_wrong: Into the page, in the same direction as the field itself

items.q: Which change would increase the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?
items.correct: Using a stronger magnet, so that the flux density is larger
items.misconception: Using much longer connecting leads between the cell and the wire
items.why: The symbol l is read simply as length of wire, with no attention paid to which part of it is in the field. Wire outside the field has no field acting on it, so it contributes no force. Doubling the length of the connecting leads changes nothing; pushing more of the wire between the poles is what increases the force.
items.random_wrong: Using a much longer wire, most of it outside the field

items.q: A straight wire carrying a current is placed so that it lies along the magnetic field lines. What is the force on the wire?
items.correct: Zero, because the wire is not at right angles to the field
items.misconception: The largest possible force, as the wire lies along the field
items.why: Lined up sounds like the best possible arrangement, as it is when two magnets attract each other. The motor effect force is perpendicular to both the current and the field, and no such direction exists when the two are parallel. Turning the wire until it is at right angles to the field gives the largest force.
items.random_wrong: Exactly the same force as when the wire is at right angles to it

items.q: For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current, which word equation gives the force on the conductor?
items.correct: force = magnetic flux density × current × length
items.misconception: force = magnetic field strength × current × length
items.why: Strength is associated with force, and force is the only magnetic quantity with a familiar unit, so the loose phrase magnetic field strength is used and given newtons. Force is measured in newtons; magnetic flux density is measured in tesla. In F = B I l the newtons appear on the left of the equation, produced by tesla × amperes × metres on the right.
items.random_wrong: force = magnetic flux density × charge × length

items.q: In the equation F = B I l, what do the symbols B and l stand for?
items.correct: B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of conductor in the field
items.misconception: B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of the whole circuit
items.why: The letter l is read as length, with no thought given to which length is meant. Only conductor inside the field contributes to the force. In a calculation the value substituted is the length of wire lying between the poles of the magnet, converted into metres.
items.random_wrong: B is the number of field lines drawn and l is the length of the wire

items.q: Which set of units should be used when the equation F = B I l is applied?
items.correct: F in newtons, B in tesla, I in amperes and l in metres
items.misconception: F in newtons, B in newtons, I in amperes and l in metres
items.why: Strength is associated with force, and force is the only magnetic quantity with a familiar unit, so the loose phrase magnetic field strength is used and given newtons. Force is measured in newtons; magnetic flux density is measured in tesla. In F = B I l the newtons appear on the left of the equation, produced by tesla × amperes × metres on the right.
items.random_wrong: F in newtons, B in tesla, I in volts and l in centimetres

items.q: A wire of length 0.30 m lies at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. The current in the wire is 2.0 A. What is the force on the wire?
items.why: With three numbers to combine, one is dropped as the calculation is written down, especially when two of them multiply neatly. Write the equation out, then substitute the numbers in the same order as the symbols. Checking that the units multiply to give newtons catches a missing quantity straight away.

items.q: A wire of length 0.30 m carries a current of 8.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field. The force on the wire is 4.8 N. What is the magnetic flux density?
items.why: The equation is remembered as a set of numbers to multiply rather than as a relation that has to be rearranged. B sits on the right-hand side of F = B I l, so it has to be made the subject first. Multiplying instead of dividing normally gives an answer far too large, which is worth checking.

items.q: A rectangular coil carrying a current is mounted on an axle between the poles of a magnet. Why does the coil tend to rotate?
items.correct: The forces on its opposite sides act in opposite directions
items.misconception: The forces on both of its sides act in the same direction, pushing it
items.why: Fleming's rule is applied once and the answer is reused for the whole coil, without noticing that the current has turned round. Follow the current round the loop: along one side it flows one way and along the opposite side it flows back. The second finger points opposite ways for the two sides, so one is pushed up while the other is pushed down, and that pair of forces turns the coil.
items.random_wrong: The coil becomes a magnet and is pulled towards the north pole

items.q: In a simple d.c. motor, what is the job of the split-ring commutator?
items.correct: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so it keeps turning one way
items.misconception: It carries the current into the coil, so that a force can act on the coil
items.why: The commutator is where the current enters, so its contact role is noticed and its switching role is missed. Plain slip rings would also carry the current in, and the coil would then stop and rock back after half a turn. The split in the ring is what swaps the connections at that moment and keeps the rotation going.
items.random_wrong: It reverses the magnetic field every half turn, so the coil keeps going

items.q: In which direction do the magnetic field lines around a straight wire run?
items.correct: They run around the wire, in circles at right angles to it.
items.misconception: They run along the wire, in the same direction as the current.
items.why: The current is the only direction marked on the circuit diagram, so the field is assumed to share it. The field is always at right angles to the current that produces it. A compass held beside the wire turns to lie across the wire, not along it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a straight current-carrying wire have a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other?
items.correct: No. Its field is a set of circles around the wire; poles at the ends belong to a bar magnet or a solenoid.
items.misconception: The wire behaves like a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
items.why: Every magnet met before this point has two poles, so poles are assumed to be a feature of anything magnetic. Poles appear where field lines leave and re-enter an object. Around a straight wire the lines simply circle it, so there is nowhere for a pole to be. Winding the wire into a solenoid is what creates ends that act as poles.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How far from a current-carrying wire does its magnetic field reach?
items.correct: The field gets weaker with distance but has no sharp edge; there is no distance at which it suddenly stops.
items.misconception: The field exists only very close to the wire and stops abruptly at the outermost circle that is drawn.
items.why: Diagrams show three or four circles and nothing beyond, so the last circle is read as a boundary. A diagram can only show a few representative lines. A sensitive compass still deflects well outside the outermost circle drawn; the field fades away gradually.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the field outside a solenoid compare with the field of a bar magnet?
items.correct: It has a similar shape, with one end of the coil acting as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
items.misconception: There is no field outside the coil at all, so a solenoid cannot be compared with a bar magnet.
items.why: Emphasis on the strong uniform field inside leads to the outside being ignored, and diagrams often stop at the coil. Field lines are closed loops, so every line inside the coil must return round the outside. A compass held beyond the end of a solenoid deflects just as it would near the pole of a bar magnet.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to an electromagnet when the current is switched off?
items.correct: The field almost completely disappears, because the iron core keeps very little magnetism.
items.misconception: The core stays magnetised permanently, so the electromagnet still works with the current switched off.
items.why: The core is seen becoming a magnet, and permanent magnets are the only kind met before, so the change is assumed to last. Iron is a soft magnetic material: it magnetises easily and loses that magnetism as soon as the field producing it is removed. Being able to switch the field off is the main advantage of an electromagnet.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the iron core in an electromagnet do?
items.correct: It is magnetised by the coil's field and adds its own field, making the total field much stronger.
items.misconception: The core carries an extra current of its own, and it is this extra current that strengthens the field.
items.why: The core is a piece of metal sitting inside a circuit, so it is assumed to join in as a conductor. The core is not part of the circuit; the wire wound on it is insulated. It strengthens the field magnetically, by having its own magnetic domains lined up by the coil's field.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A wire carrying a current becomes warm. Does this show that it produces a magnetic field?
items.correct: No. Warming shows energy transferred by heating; the magnetic effect is shown by a compass deflecting.
items.misconception: The wire warming up is evidence for the magnetic effect of the current.
items.why: Both effects appear when the current is switched on, so any observed change is taken as evidence for whichever effect is being discussed. A heating effect occurs in any resistor, including ones whose field is far too weak to notice. Only a magnetic test object, such as a plotting compass or iron filings, tests for a magnetic field.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the field lines at the ends of a solenoid?
items.correct: They continue out of the end, loop round the outside and re-enter at the other end, forming closed loops.
items.misconception: The lines start at one end of the coil and stop at the other end.
items.why: Diagrams often show only the inside of the coil, and lines that end at the edge of a drawing look like lines that end. Magnetic field lines never begin or end anywhere. Continuing each line round the outside is exactly what gives the solenoid its bar-magnet shape and its poles.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a solenoid work by trapping the magnetic field lines inside the coil?
items.correct: No. The lines pass out of the ends and loop round outside; the coil concentrates the field, it does not trap it.
items.misconception: The turns of wire enclose the field so that none of it can escape from the coil.
items.why: A container holding something in is an easy way to explain why the field inside is strong. If nothing escaped there would be no external field and no poles, yet a compass clearly deflects near the end of a solenoid. The field inside is strong because contributions add, not because they are shut in.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an electromagnet attract or repel the iron armature in a relay or a bell?
items.correct: It attracts it, because the iron is magnetised so that the end nearest the coil is an opposite pole.
items.misconception: The electromagnet repels the armature and pushes it onto the contacts.
items.why: Magnets are remembered as both attracting and repelling, so either seems possible here. Repulsion needs two magnets with like poles facing. The armature is unmagnetised iron, and induced magnetism always produces an opposite pole facing the magnet, so the force can only be attraction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In which direction does the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field act?
items.correct: At right angles to both the current and the field, in the direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
items.misconception: Along the field lines, in the same direction as the magnetic field.
items.why: Forces between magnets act along the line joining them, so the force is expected to follow the field here too. The motor effect force is perpendicular to both the current and the field. Fleming's left-hand rule sets the three directions mutually at right angles, which is why the wire jumps out of the gap rather than along it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the force on the conductor act along the wire?
items.correct: No. It acts at right angles to the wire, so the wire is pushed sideways out of the field.
items.misconception: The force pushes the wire along its own length, in the direction of the current.
items.why: The current is the most obvious direction in the problem, and a push is assumed to act the way things are already moving. Fleming's left-hand rule holds the thumb at right angles to the second finger, so the force can never lie along the current. In a demonstration the wire swings sideways across the gap between the poles.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which hand is used for the motor effect?
items.correct: The left hand. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force on a current-carrying conductor in a field.
items.misconception: The right hand is used, since the right-hand grip rule was used for the field around a wire.
items.why: Several hand rules are met close together and are stored as one vague hand rule. The right hand is for the grip rule and for the generator effect; the left hand is for the motor effect. The two hands give opposite answers, so the choice changes the predicted direction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How can the force on a conductor in a magnetic field be made larger?
items.correct: Increase the current, use a magnet of larger flux density, or put more of the conductor in the field.
items.misconception: Reduce the current so that less energy is wasted heating the wire, leaving more available for the force.
items.why: Energy-saving language from earlier electricity work is imported into a question about the size of a force. F = B I l says the force is proportional to the current, so reducing the current reduces the force. Heating is a separate effect and takes nothing away from the magnetic force.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the equation for the force on a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field?
items.correct: force = magnetic flux density × current × length.
items.misconception: force = magnetic flux density × charge × length, using charge in place of current.
items.why: Charge and current both describe the flow of electrons and are treated as interchangeable words. The quantity in the equation is current, measured in amperes, not charge measured in coulombs. Substituting a charge gives an answer that is not in newtons, which is a quick check on the mistake.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In F = B I l, what does the symbol B stand for?
items.correct: The magnetic flux density of the field, measured in tesla.
items.misconception: The number of magnetic field lines drawn on the diagram.
items.why: Diagrams show more lines for a stronger field, so the count of lines is taken to be the quantity itself. The number of lines drawn is a choice made by whoever drew the diagram. Flux density is a measured quantity in tesla, shown by how closely the lines are spaced rather than by how many are drawn.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the unit of the current in F = B I l?
items.correct: The ampere, A; amp is acceptable for ampere.
items.misconception: The volt, V, because the supply is what drives the circuit.
items.why: Voltage is the number written on the power supply, so it is the electrical quantity most readily recalled. Current is measured in amperes and read on an ammeter placed in series with the conductor. The potential difference does not appear anywhere in this equation.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A wire of length 30 cm is in a magnetic field. What value of l is substituted into F = B I l?
items.correct: 0.30 m, because the length must be substituted in metres.
items.misconception: 30, using the number exactly as it is given in centimetres.
items.why: The number is copied straight from the question without checking it against the unit list for the equation. The specification gives length, l, in metres, m. Substituting centimetres makes the answer 100 times too large, which is usually obvious when the answer is compared with everyday forces.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the coil in a motor rotate because it is attracted to one of the magnet's poles?
items.correct: No. It rotates because of the motor-effect forces on its current-carrying sides.
items.misconception: The coil becomes a magnet and is pulled bodily towards the north pole of the magnet.
items.why: Attraction between poles is the familiar magnetic explanation and is reached for before the motor effect is considered. The coil turns on a fixed axle and does not move towards either pole. What acts on it is a pair of equal forces in opposite directions on opposite sides, which produces rotation and no overall pull.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is clamped so that it cannot move. Is there a force on it?
items.correct: Yes. The force acts whether or not the wire is free to move; clamping it simply stops it accelerating.
items.misconception: There is no force until the wire is released and allowed to move about.
items.why: Force is identified with visible movement, so a stationary object is assumed to have no force on it. A clamped wire pushes on its clamp, and a magnet resting on a balance shows a change in reading when the current flows. The force is present; the wire is simply held in place by a second force.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is it that reverses every half turn in a simple d.c. motor?
items.correct: The direction of the current in the coil, reversed by the split-ring commutator.
items.misconception: The magnetic field reverses every half turn while the current stays the same.
items.why: Something clearly has to reverse for the coil to keep turning, and the field is the other direction in the problem. The field comes from a fixed permanent magnet and cannot reverse. The split ring turns with the coil and swaps which brush feeds which side, so it is the current in the coil that reverses.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
